item.title: AI Agents in November: The Reality Check
item.description: This comprehensive review covers 159 articles published in November 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI agents. This month brought a crucial reality check for AI agents. Multiple independent studies revealed agents struggling to work autonomously, Microsoft bet big on “Agent 365” as an operating system for AI agents, and security researchers documented the first cases of malicious agent use. Yet amid the sobering news, real deployments showed tangible results.
item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 159 articles published in November 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI agents. This month brought a crucial reality check for AI agents. Multiple independent studies revealed agents struggling to work autonomously, Microsoft bet big on “Agent 365” as an operating system for AI agents, and security researchers documented the first cases of malicious agent use. Yet amid the sobering news, real deployments showed tangible results.

The Performance Reality Check

The most significant story this month was the mounting evidence that AI agents, as currently built, cannot work independently. A landmark study from Upwork drew from more than 300 real client projects and found that AI agents routinely fail to complete even straightforward professional tasks on their own. The research tested leading models—Gemini 2.5 Pro, OpenAI’s GPT-5, and ClaudeSonnet 4—on actual jobs posted by paying clients.

The results were stark. When working alone, AI agents showed low completion rates across the board. For data science and analytics projects, ClaudeSonnet 4 achieved a 64% completion rate independently but jumped to 93% after receiving feedback from a human expert. In sales and marketing work, Gemini 2.5 Pro’s completion rate rose from 17% independently to 31% with human input . OpenAI’s GPT-5 showed similarly dramatic improvements in engineering tasks, climbing from 30% to 50% completion with human oversight .

When AI agents collaborate with human experts, project completion rates surge by up to 70% . This finding challenges the fundamental assumption in the AI industry that agent benchmarks conducted in isolation accurately predict real-world performance.

Microsoft’s own testing yielded similar disappointing results. Researchers built a synthetic marketplace called the “Magentic Marketplace” to test AI agent behavior, with 100 customer-side agents interacting with 300 business-side agents. The experiments using models like GPT-4o, GPT-5, and Gemini-2.5-Flash found agents were vulnerable to manipulation and overwhelmed by having too many options . The agents also struggled with collaboration without explicit instructions.

A separate benchmark called the Remote Labor Index (RLI) showed that current AI agents perform poorly when automating real remote jobs, with top models automating only 2.5% or less of complex work valued at over $140,000.

Harvard Business Review reached a complementary conclusion: agents aren’t ready for consumer-facing work but can excel at internal processes . The analysis suggests agents work better for internal workflows where errors can be caught and corrected, rather than customer-facing interactions where mistakes directly impact brand and revenue.

Even the mainstream press is noticing. The Hill reported that “AI agents aren’t replacing remote workers any time soon,” citing the mounting evidence of performance limitations.

This reality check sets the stage for everything else that happened in November. The industry is building infrastructure for agents that don’t yet exist as promised capabilities—but the gap between vision and reality is becoming clearer.

Microsoft’s Agent Operating System

While studies showed agents struggling in practice, Microsoft made its biggest bet yet on the agentic future. At its Ignite 2025 conference, the company unveiled a comprehensive vision to turn Windows into an “agentic OS” with Agent 365 as the management layer.

Agent 365 is a control plane framework for businesses to securely deploy, manage, and monitor AI agents “like they do people.” The platform provides dashboards, telemetry, and security controls for managing fleets of AI bots. A Microsoft executive quoted in CNBC predicted a future where companies use far more AI agents than human employees.

The portfolio Microsoft announced is extensive:

  • Agent 365: The central management platform for AI agents across the enterprise
  • Fara-7B: A 7-billion parameter AI agent designed to perform complex computer tasks directly on a user’s device; rivals GPT-4o in benchmark performance and processes data locally for privacy
  • Entra Agent ID: Identity documentation for AI agents, treating them like a digital workforce with their own identities
  • Windows integration: Microsoft is transforming Windows 11 into an “agentic OS” by integrating AI agents directly into the taskbar and File Explorer
  • Magentic Marketplace: An open source simulation environment for testing AI agent behavior
  • Microsoft Foundry: A modular, interoperable, and secure agent stack for building and scaling AI agents

eWeek called it “the Operating System for AI Agents.” The vision is clear: Microsoft wants to be the platform layer for the agentic era, just as Windows was for the PC era.

But not everyone is convinced this is what enterprises want. PCMag asked whether anyone actually wants to create their own AI agents, questioning whether the vision aligns with enterprise needs. Computerworld noted the tool is designed to help IT manage “AI agent sprawl”—suggesting agents are proliferating faster than organizations can manage them.

Product Purpose Status
Agent 365 Manage AI agents like digital workforce Launched
Fara-7B On-device computer-use agent for PCs Launched
Entra Agent ID Identity & access control for agents Preview
Magentic Marketplace Agent marketplace and testing environment Open Source
Copilot Agents Azure agent building tools Updated

Microsoft’s announcement also included security tools, reflecting growing awareness of the risks that come with autonomous agents. The company announced autonomous security capabilities for AI agents and partnerships with security vendors like Wiz to secure the agentic environment.

The Ignite announcements weren’t limited to agents—Microsoft also unveiled updates to Azure Copilot agents, AI infrastructure innovations, and integrations with partners like Adobe, Nvidia, ServiceNow, and Workday. But agents were clearly the centerpiece, reflecting Microsoft’s belief that agentic AI represents the next major shift in enterprise computing.

Security Challenges Mount

As Microsoft and others build out agent infrastructure, security researchers are documenting serious risks. November brought multiple revelations about how agents can be exploited—or how they can exploit each other.

Documented Attacks

The most concerning report came from Axios: Chinese hackers used Anthropic’s Claude Code agent to automate spying operations . The attackers, associated with a group called “Suspended Packages,” used Anthropic’s own AI agent to identify vulnerable files, exfiltrate data, and maintain persistence on compromised systems. This is one of the first documented cases of malicious actors using AI agents as attack tools.

Another concerning finding came from security researchers who discovered that ServiceNow AI agents can be tricked into acting against each other via “second-order prompts.” By crafting prompts that cause one agent to interpret another agent’s actions as hostile, attackers can trigger agent-vs-agent conflicts that disrupt operations.

Medium raised questions about whether Windows 11’s new AI agents represent “convenience or a new attack vector,” noting that agents with deep system access could be exploited if compromised.

Enterprise Readiness Gap

Despite these documented risks, enterprises are not prepared. ZDNET reported that “enterprises are not prepared for a world of malicious AI agents,” citing a lack of governance frameworks and security controls. A separate analysis in The AI Economy found that while enterprises anticipate a 2027 AI agent explosion, “reality shows they’re not ready.”

The IAPP (International Association of Privacy Professionals) published two analyses on the topic: one on understanding new risks and practical safeguards and another on considerations for tackling agentic AI risks . Both emphasized that current privacy and security frameworks were not designed for autonomous agents that can access, move, and alter data without human oversight.

CIO summarized the sentiment bluntly: “Agentic AI has big trust issues.”

Security Infrastructure

The market is responding with new security tools and frameworks:

  • Runlayer launched out of stealth with $11 million in seed funding from Khosla Ventures’ Keith Rabois and Felicis. The startup addresses security vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the standard for AI agent connectivity. It has already signed eight unicorns as customers .

  • Ping Identity launched “Identity for AI” , a solution designed to provide identity verification for AI agents in what the company calls the “agent economy.”

  • Keycard, an AI agent identity startup, acquired Runebook to strengthen its MCP connectivity capabilities.

  • Nokod Security launched Adaptive Agent Security to protect AI agents across the entire agent development lifecycle.

  • Wiz unveiled multiple agent security products , including a SecOps AI Agent and AI-SPM for securing AI agents.

  • AWS published The Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix , a framework for securing autonomous AI systems.

  • GitHub published its agentic security principles for building secure AI agents.

  • Forrester released Applying Forrester’s AEGIS Framework To IAM And AI Agents , a framework for identity and access management in the age of agents.

  • AvePoint debuted AgentPulse Command Center for AI agent governance.

  • BleepingComputer explored how “Never Trust, Always Verify” applies to autonomous AI agents.

  • SlashData published guidance on how to harness AI agents without breaking security .

  • New America examined privacy and power in the Model Context Protocol era.

  • Dark Reading warned that “AI Agents Are Going Rogue” and offered strategies to rein them in.

  • SC Media argued that AI agents could end security’s cycle of toil—if properly managed.

  • The Hacker News explored how to govern AI agents “from enterprise risk to strategic asset.”

The security challenge is becoming clear: as agents gain more autonomy and access, they become both more valuable and more dangerous. The industry is racing to build guardrails before deployments scale beyond control.

Real-World Deployments

Despite the performance limitations and security concerns, real deployments are showing results. The most cited example this month was Klarna, which reported that its AI agent is doing the work of 853 employees . This represents significant productivity—but notably, it’s in customer service, a well-defined domain with clear processes and human oversight available.

Capgemini found that banks and insurers are deploying AI agents to fight fraud and process applications, with plans for new roles specifically to supervise the AI. The report indicates that financial institutions are actively moving key customer-facing processes to AI agents, marking a rapid transformation in how customers interact with banks and insurers. CIO Dive reported that banks are creating “AI supervisor” roles as agent use surges.

Amazon Connect launched AI agents capable of autonomous action for customer service, representing a step beyond simple chatbots toward agents that can take actions on behalf of customers.

In the public sector, Staffordshire Police announced it will trial AI agents on 101 service —the non-emergency police contact line—marking one of the first tests of agents in a government service context. Axios reported exclusively that the IRS has deployed AI agents for internal operations.

Tearsheet podcasted about “AI agents making real financial decisions,” featuring NVIDIA’s Kevin Levitt on the infrastructure behind live deployments at Capital One, Visa, and RBC.

Sage debuted a Finance Intelligence AI Agent for financial workflows. Zeni rolled out an AI agent to automate complex accounting workloads.

Oracle’s Clinical AI Agent clicked quickly for Hudson Physicians, showing results in healthcare. Fast Company explored how AI agents are about to change how people shop, with implications for retail.

The Wall Street Journal reported that “companies begin to see a return on AI agents,” citing early adopters showing measurable ROI. PYMNTS.com published guidance on “What CFOs Should Be Asking About AI Agents,” reflecting finance leaders’ need to understand and justify the investments.

But there are challenges in deployment as well. Ad Age reported on how AI agents are “messing with ad metrics” as Amazon fights Perplexity over undeclared bots. The agents don’t shop like humans, and they don’t view ads like humans—creating measurement headaches for digital advertising.

Company Use Case Results
Klarna Customer service Handling work of 853 employees
Banks & Insurers Fraud detection & application processing Live deployment with new supervisor roles
Staffordshire Police 101 service triage Trial phase
IRS Internal operations Deployed
Amazon Connect Customer service agents Autonomous action capability

The pattern is clear: the deployments that work are specialized, well-defined, and include human oversight. These aren’t autonomous agents replacing humans—they’re tools augmenting humans in specific contexts.

Industry Activity

Beyond the headlines, activity continued across sectors:

Financial Services & Commerce

  • Gartner predicted that AI agents will command $15 trillion in B2B purchases by 2028 , representing a massive shift in how business buying happens.

  • Quantum Metric partnered with Google Cloud to accelerate its push into the AI agent marketplace , leveraging Google’s Gemini and Agent2Agent protocol.

  • Ad Age reported on how AI agents are threatening retail media ad strategies as Amazon fights Perplexity over undeclared bots.

  • AWS published on “decoding the future of retail: embracing AI shopping agents.”

  • The World Economic Forum covered “the rise and risks of AI shopping agents.”

  • Marketing Brew reported on how brands are aiming to build “algorithmic trust” ahead of an AI agent-powered Black Friday.

  • PYMNTS.com published on how “AI agents take over the SEO playbook.”

  • RCR Wireless argued that telecom’s next billion-dollar customer is an AI agent.

Technology Platforms

  • GoDaddy advanced trusted AI agent identity with its Agent Name Service (ANS) API and standards site launch.

  • Refinder AI Agent brought end-to-end task automation to Slack and Google Chat.

  • Celonis feeds AI agents with process intelligence data to enhance their operational context.

  • Everbridge introduced an AI agent in xMatters to accelerate digital service resilience.

  • Komodor extended its autonomous AI agent for optimizing Kubernetes clusters.

  • Gluware tackled AI agent coordination with its Titan platform.

  • WorkFusion partnered with Allied Engineering Group to expand AI agent adoption across the Middle East and Africa .

  • Fujitsu discussed pioneering the future of business with generative AI and AI agents.

Technology Development

  • NVIDIA published on building an interactive AI agent and how to build and run secure, data-driven AI agents .

  • MIT researchers developed an AI agent that learns to use CAD to create 3D objects from sketches.

  • EPAM mapped the GenAI coding landscape, identifying five types of AI agents in the development stack.

  • DevOps.com covered AI agent performance testing in the DevOps pipeline.

  • Salesforce unveiled a simulation environment for training AI agents called DreamGym.

  • AWS introduced Strands Agent SOPs —natural language workflows for AI agents.

  • SAP Signavio launched Agent Mining to transform enterprise AI.

  • Deutsche Telekom announced AI agents for mobile networks.

  • CX Today published on how AI co-pilots are powering the next generation of “super agents.”

Sector-Specific

  • Infosys developed an AI agent to enhance operations in the energy sector.

  • Supply & Demand Chain Executive covered readying AI agents for procurement.

  • Crowe examined AI agents as the next shift in manufacturing.

  • Bloomberg reported that China’s top companies are focusing on AI agents as the next battleground.

  • CIO provided a change management guide for preparing workforces for AI agents.

  • S&P Global found that AI agents worsen IT’s capacity crunch.

Infrastructure & Tooling

New Agent Launches

  • Neuron7 launched Neuro , a next-gen AI agent for mission-critical service resolution.

  • Ironclad unveiled its next wave of AI agents for legal agreements.

  • Cresta unveiled four products at Cresta Wave for human and AI agent collaboration.

  • Smartsheet unveiled its AI agent platform to elevate productivity and collaboration.

  • Writer announced AI agents that can “actually do your work—not just chat about it.”

  • Time Magazine launched an AI-driven interactive agent, with Axios reporting exclusively on the launch.

  • Intuit introduced a virtual team of AI agents to help UK businesses increase efficiency and growth.

  • ECI Software Solutions launched a built-in ecommerce AI agent.

  • Ingram Micro launched an AI agent in its Xvantage platform.

Platform & Tool Updates

  • Google Cloud updated its AI Agent Builder with new observability dashboard and faster build-and-deploy tools.

  • InfoWorld reported on Google boosting Vertex AI Agent Builder.

  • Google announced the Agent Development Kit for Go.

  • Google DeepMind released SIMA 2 , a Gemini-powered AI agent for 3D virtual worlds.

  • Google published on building AI agents with Gemini 3 and open source frameworks.

  • Google rolled out new guardrails for AI agents.

  • Databricks added customizable evaluation tools to boost AI agent accuracy.

  • AWS showcased enterprise AI agent solutions with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

  • AWS explained how Letta builds production-ready AI agents with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.

  • Oracle announced its AI Agent Marketplace.

  • InfoWorld published on the anatomy of an AI agent knowledge base.

  • The Journal of Accountancy covered creating an AI agent in ChatGPT.

  • Anthropic published on code execution with MCP for building more efficient AI agents.

  • The New Stack examined why load tests lie about AI agent performance.

Market Infrastructure

  • IAB launched a technical standard for faster, AI agent-friendly ad auctions.

Measuring What Works

As enterprises deploy agents, they’re discovering that measurement and governance are prerequisites for success.

Snowflake proposed a “GPA framework” for evaluating AI agent reliability, treating agent assessment like academic grading with metrics across multiple dimensions of performance.

SaaStr reported on 125 days and 750,000 uses of AI agents, concluding that while agents are now “truly part of the team,” their moats are “real but weak.” The same analysis noted that SaaStr runs 20+ AI agents and found their competitive advantages are modest.

MarTech reported that “most AI agents fail without data and governance maturity,” emphasizing that technical capability alone doesn’t ensure successful deployment.

McKinsey published “The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation,” providing a comprehensive overview of enterprise AI adoption. A separate McKinsey report, “Agents for growth” , examined turning AI promise into business impact.

AP News published a reality check titled “‘Agentic’ AI is a buzzword made up of marketing fluff and real promise,” distinguishing between hype and actual capability.

CIO explored measuring and scaling AI agent value beyond productivity gains.

IBM published on “Enterprise AI Agents: Beyond Productivity,” arguing that value comes from rethinking workflows, not just automating existing tasks.

ERP Today covered how AI agents are shifting from hype to enterprise workflow redesign.

DataRobot argued that IT needs to manage AI agents like a workforce.

The Takeaway

November 2025 was a reality check month for AI agents. The hype is meeting reality in three important ways.

First, agents work in narrow contexts with human oversight, not as autonomous replacements. The Upwork study, Microsoft’s marketplace test, and the Remote Labor Index all show the same thing: current AI agents struggle independently but excel with human partners. The deployments that work—Klarna’s customer service agent, banks using AI for fraud detection, Amazon Connect’s autonomous agents—are specialized tools, not general-purpose replacements.

Second, Microsoft’s infrastructure bet suggests the company sees this as a long-term play requiring new OS-level capabilities. Agent 365, Fara-7B, Entra Agent ID, and the Windows “agentic OS” transformation represent a massive investment in the agent platform layer. This is infrastructure build-out, not breakthrough capability. Microsoft is building the roads before the cars are ready.

Third, security challenges are real and escalating. Documented cases of Chinese hackers using Anthropic’s agent for automated spying and ServiceNow agents being tricked into fighting each other show that autonomous agents create new attack surfaces. The rapid emergence of security startups like Runlayer, Nokod, and established players like Wiz and Ping Identity launching agent security products indicates this will be a significant growth area.

The deployments that show results share common characteristics: well-defined domains, clear processes, abundant training data, and human oversight. These aren’t the science fiction autonomous agents that make decisions without context—they’re specialized tools that excel at specific tasks.

Gartner’s $15 trillion prediction for B2B purchases by AI agents in 2028 shows the stakes. But enterprises anticipating a 2027 agent explosion may be premature. The AI Economy found that organizations aren’t ready for the risks.

We’re in the infrastructure build-out phase, not the autonomous agent phase. Forrester’s 2026 predictions underscore that this is a multi-year transition. The winners will be companies that focus on practical deployment in narrow contexts, build robust governance frameworks, and integrate agents as collaborators rather than replacements.

The age of AI agents is coming. But November 2025 showed it’s coming more slowly—and more collaboratively—than the hype suggested.

item.title: AI Agents in September: Google's Payments Protocol, Billion-Dollar Funding, and Growing Security Concerns
item.description: This comprehensive review covers 205 articles published in September 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI agents. Google launched an open payments protocol enabling autonomous agent-to-agent transactions. Startups raised over $1 billion in funding, led by Sierra’s $350M round and Cognition’s $400M raise. But as enterprises deploy agents at scale, security vulnerabilities emerged—researchers disclosed 25 critical vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol, and Salesforce revealed AI agents can be forced to leak sensitive data.
item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 205 articles published in September 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI agents. Google launched an open payments protocol enabling autonomous agent-to-agent transactions. Startups raised over $1 billion in funding, led by Sierra’s $350M round and Cognition’s $400M raise. But as enterprises deploy agents at scale, security vulnerabilities emerged—researchers disclosed 25 critical vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol, and Salesforce revealed AI agents can be forced to leak sensitive data.

The Infrastructure Play

Google launched an open payments protocol enabling AI agents to transact directly with one another, using stablecoins for settlement. The protocol allows autonomous agents to commerce without human intervention—a foundational capability for the agentic economy. As American Banker noted , banks need to understand how this protocol could transform payment infrastructure when agents become economic actors.

The protocol addresses a core bottleneck in agentic systems: agents can’t autonomously buy and sell without payment capabilities. Google’s solution uses stablecoins to enable instant settlement, giving agents a way to hold and transfer value. Ledger Insights reported that this represents one of the first major infrastructure plays for agent-to-agent commerce at scale.

Visa also moved into the agentic commerce space, introducing new tools for developers building AI agents that engage in commerce. The company’s Instant Checkout and Agentic Commerce Protocol aim to standardize how agents participate in retail transactions.

OpenAI announced Instant Checkout and an Agentic Commerce Protocol, enabling ChatGPT to complete purchases directly within conversations. The integration removes friction from AI-assisted shopping—agents can now move from recommendation to transaction without switching contexts.

Mastercard released a guide to agentic retail , explaining how “agentic commerce” works and what retailers need to prepare for as AI agents become shopping assistants. The company framed agents as the next evolution of e-commerce, where AI handles discovery, comparison, and purchase on behalf of consumers.

This infrastructure layer matters because it enables the agent economy to function. Agents need to transact autonomously to be useful—from buying supplies to paying for API calls. September’s developments suggest the payment rails are being built in parallel with agent capabilities.

Billion-Dollar Bet

AI agent startups raised over $1.1 billion in September 2025, with two mega-rounds dominating the landscape and a long tail of specialized vertical applications attracting funding.

Mega-Rounds: Horizontal Platforms

Sierra raised $350 million at a $10 billion valuation, led by Greenoaks Capital. The company, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, builds customer service AI agents for enterprises. The $10B valuation places Sierra among the most valuable private AI agent companies, reflecting investor confidence in horizontal agent platforms that can serve multiple enterprise use cases.

Cognition raised $400 million to bolster its AI agent efforts. The company, known for its Devin software engineering agent, is building horizontal AI agents for coding and development tasks. The round brings total funding to nearly $1B for the company, which competes in the crowded AI software engineering space.

Vertical Specialists: Finance & Operations

Motion raised $60 million for AI agents designed for small businesses. TechCrunch reported Motion is building “the Microsoft Office of AI agents”—a suite of agents for common business workflows. The company is Y Combinator-backed and targets small business productivity with result-based pricing.

Tabs raised $55 million for AI agents serving finance teams. The company’s agents automate financial workflows, reconciliation, and reporting—targeting a pain point that requires accuracy and compliance. The round reflects investor interest in vertical AI agents that solve specific business problems.

Paid raised a $21 million seed round for a “results-based billing” model for AI agents. Founded by Manny Medina (former Outreach CEO), Paid only charges when its agents successfully complete tasks. The unusual pricing model addresses enterprise skepticism about AI agent ROI—customers pay for outcomes, not seat licenses. Lightspeed and FUSE led the round, with Lightspeed publishing an analysis of the "$19 trillion problem" in the AI agent economy that Paid aims to solve.

Seed Stage: Infrastructure & Security

Envive raised $15 million to build AI agents for online retailers. The Seattle startup’s agents handle customer service, product recommendations, and post-purchase support for e-commerce sites.

InCountry raised $10 million and launched AgentCloak, an AI agent data protection platform. The company’s technology helps enterprises comply with data residency regulations when agents cross borders—addressing a looming compliance challenge as agents access data globally.

Geordie emerged from stealth with $6.5 million for an AI agent security platform. The startup focuses on securing agent deployments, reflecting growing concern about agent vulnerabilities.

uiAgent raised $4.6 million to accelerate AI agent automation for accounting firms. The company’s agents handle tax preparation, bookkeeping, and client communication—addressing the accounting industry’s labor shortage.

Actual AI raised $3.2 million to build AI agents for engineering managers. The agents help with code reviews, sprint planning, and team coordination.

The funding pattern is clear: investors are betting on specific vertical applications (HR, accounting, finance, security) rather than general “agent platforms.” Sierra and Cognition are the outliers—horizontal agent platforms commanding premium valuations. Most capital is flowing to companies solving concrete business problems with agents, not building general-purpose agent infrastructure.

Enterprise Product Launches

September saw a flood of enterprise agent product announcements as major technology companies integrated agents into existing product suites. The pattern was consistent: vendors are embedding agents into productivity software, not selling standalone agent products. The “agentification” of enterprise software is underway.

Company Agent Product Use Case
Amazon Ad Agent Create ads from start to finish
Microsoft Office Agents Word, Excel, PowerPoint automation
Oracle 13 HR Agents HR automation and performance
Notion Workflow Agents Research, write, run workflows
Workday HR/Finance Agents Contingent work, finance, industries
Box Content Agents Content management workflows
Adobe Customer Experience Agents Orchestrate customer journeys
Salesforce MuleSoft Agent Fabric Enterprise infrastructure

Amazon: Ads & Seller Experience

Amazon debuted an AI agent that can create ads from start to finish for its platforms. As ADWEEK reported , the ad agent handles creative generation, copywriting, and campaign management—reducing the friction for advertisers to launch campaigns on Amazon’s properties.

The company also launched a seller agent to help third-party sellers manage their businesses. According to Amazon’s announcement, the agent helps with inventory management, pricing decisions, and customer service—tasks that previously required significant seller time. CNBC noted the agent arrives as sellers face supply chain disruptions and trade policy uncertainty, making automation more attractive.

Microsoft: Office 365 & Teams

Microsoft added AI agents to Word, Excel, and PowerPoint , extending Copilot from chat interface to autonomous action. The agents can research, draft documents, analyze data, and create presentations—handling multi-step workflows that previously required human direction.

The company also filled Teams with AI agents , including agents for meeting preparation, recap, and follow-up tasks. Microsoft’s blog announced “Agent Mode and Office Agent” in Microsoft 365 Copilot, positioning agents as the evolution of productivity software.

HR & Workforce Management

Oracle expanded Fusion HCM with 13 new AI agents for HR automation. The agents handle performance reviews, career pathing, onboarding, and employee questions—automating many routine HR tasks while providing insights to managers. Oracle’s announcement positioned the agents as “AI-powered HR assistants” that boost workforce productivity and enhance performance management.

Workday expanded AI agents to HR, Finance, and specific industries . The company launched Workday Data Cloud and Workday Build, alongside more AI agents for contingent work, finance operations, and industry-specific workflows. Staffing Industry Analysts noted that Workday’s new agents include one specifically focused on contingent work—reflecting the growing gig economy workforce.

Indeed unveiled AI agents for job seekers and recruiters . The job platform’s agents help candidates find relevant openings, prepare applications, and practice interviews—while giving recruiters tools to screen candidates and schedule interviews automatically.

Productivity & Content

Notion launched AI agents that can research, write, and run workflows . The company’s workflow agents handle knowledge management, content creation, and task automation—extending Notion from a note-taking tool into an autonomous work platform. The agent can research topics across the web, draft documents, and execute multi-step workflows within Notion.

Box debuted AI agents for content management . The agents handle document classification, metadata extraction, contract analysis, and content routing—addressing the enterprise challenge of managing unstructured data at scale.

Adobe announced general availability of AI agents for customer experience orchestration. The company’s Agent Orchestrator and AI agents help businesses create personalized customer journeys across channels. As CIO reported , Adobe’s agents can analyze customer behavior, trigger personalized experiences, and coordinate across marketing, sales, and service touchpoints.

Genesys launched AI agents with greater autonomy for customer experience orchestration. The contact center platform’s agents handle customer inquiries, resolve issues, and escalate complex cases to humans—operating with more independence than previous chatbot-style systems.

ServiceNow launched the Zurich release, inserting process and task mining into AI agent workflows. The integration gives agents visibility into business processes, allowing them to identify bottlenecks and optimization opportunities.

The enterprise launch wave shows that incumbents are integrating agents into existing products rather than creating standalone agent platforms. This approach reduces adoption friction—users get agent capabilities within tools they already use. But it also means agents will be embedded in proprietary ecosystems, raising questions about interoperability and data portability.

Security Reality Check

As enterprises deploy AI agents at scale, security vulnerabilities have emerged that could undermine trust in the technology. September brought sobering news: researchers disclosed 25 critical vulnerabilities in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Salesforce revealed AI agents can be manipulated to leak sensitive data, and reports surfaced of malicious agent servers stealing emails.

Critical Vulnerabilities Exposed

Security researchers found 25 vulnerabilities in MCP , the protocol that enables AI agents to connect to external tools and data sources. The vulnerabilities expose how agents can be exploited through the protocol itself—raising questions about whether the foundation of agent infrastructure is secure.

The MCP vulnerabilities are particularly concerning because the protocol is rapidly becoming a standard for agent-tool integration. If agents can’t safely connect to tools without being exploited, the entire agent ecosystem faces a bottleneck. The disclosures came as the World Economic Forum warned that unsecured AI agents expose businesses to new cyberthreats.

Salesforce disclosed that its AI agents can be forced to leak sensitive data . Researchers found that adversarial inputs can trick agents into bypassing security controls and exposing information they shouldn’t. The disclosure is notable because Salesforce has been aggressive in deploying agents—CEO Marc Benioff said agents now handle 50% of the company’s work.

Reports emerged of a malicious AI agent server stealing emails . The incident highlights how bad actors are already weaponizing agent infrastructure—creating rogue agents that exfiltrate data under the guise of legitimate AI services.

Additional research found that seemingly harmless photos could be used to hack AI agents . The attack technique involves embedding malicious instructions in images that agents process—bypassing text-based filters. TechRadar warned that IT can’t afford blind trust when agents go rogue.

CISOs Not Ready

Fast Company reported that AI agents are “breaking bad” and CISOs aren’t ready . The article documented how security teams lack visibility into agent behavior, can’t audit agent decisions, and don’t have tools to police agent-to-agent interactions. Help Net Security similarly noted that “AI agents are here, now comes the hard part for CISOs.”

Zscaler’s analysis examined the challenge of balancing speed and security in AI agent deployments—arguing that security can’t be an afterthought when agents have access to sensitive systems and data.

Computer Weekly asked whether AI agents are a blessing or curse for cybersecurity. The article noted that while agents can help defend systems, they also create new attack surfaces that defenders must monitor and protect.

Industry Response: New Security Platforms

The industry is responding with new security platforms and governance frameworks:

Astrix Security announced the first AI Agent Control Plane (ACP) for secure-by-design agent deployment. The ACP provides centralized visibility into agent permissions, data access, and connections—giving security teams a way to police agent behavior at scale. The Hacker News described how Astrix’s platform helps secure the “agentic era.”

Airia launched Agent Constraints , the industry’s first policy engine for centralized AI agent governance. The platform lets enterprises set guardrails on what agents can do, what data they can access, and how decisions are reviewed—addressing the control problem that plagues agent deployments.

Covasant launched an AI Agent Control Tower to “bring order to the chaotic enterprise AI landscape.” The platform provides visibility, governance, and management capabilities for enterprises running multiple agents from different vendors.

Geordie’s $6.5 million seed round for an AI agent security platform reflects growing investment in agent security as a category.

Lasso Platform employs AI agents to secure AI applications , using agent technology to police agent behavior—a “fight fire with fire” approach to security.

The Hacker News published guidance on how to gain control of AI agents and non-human identities, noting that traditional identity management approaches don’t work when agents create their own sub-identities and permissions.

CrowdStrike debuted threat-hunting AI agents and partnered with Salesforce on security solutions for AI agents and applications. The company is positioning itself as a security provider for the agentic era.

Wipro integrated Simbian’s AI agent into its managed security services, reflecting how security providers are incorporating agents into their operations.

What September Means

September 2025 marked a phase transition for AI agents—from concept to deployment, from experimental to essential. The developments of the month reveal five patterns shaping the agentic future.

1. Infrastructure First

The industry is building rails before running fast. Google’s payments protocol, Visa’s commerce tools, and the emergence of governance platforms all suggest that infrastructure is being laid before explosive adoption. This is the opposite of typical tech hype cycles—usually products come first, infrastructure second. The agent ecosystem is being built methodically, with payment protocols, security platforms, and governance frameworks emerging alongside the first generation of products.

2. Verticalization Wins

Investors are funding specific use cases, not general agent platforms. Sierra and Cognition are exceptions that prove the rule—horizontal platforms at eye-popping valuations. But most capital is flowing to vertical applications: accounting (uiAgent, Paid), finance (Tabs), retail (Envive), healthcare (Hyro), security (Geordie). The pattern suggests enterprises want agents that understand their industry, not general-purpose assistants that require extensive customization.

3. Security Is the Bottleneck

The MCP vulnerabilities and Salesforce data leaks are setbacks, but they’re also forcing the industry to take security seriously. The rapid emergence of security platforms (Astrix ACP, Airia Agent Constraints, Covasant Control Tower) suggests vendors are treating security as a product requirement, not an afterthought. The question is whether security can catch up to deployment speed—CISOs clearly aren’t ready, as Fast Company reported, but the tools to address the gap are appearing rapidly.

4. Enterprise Integration Is Key

Microsoft, Oracle, Workday, Amazon, Notion, Box, Adobe— incumbents are embedding agents into existing products, not selling standalone agent platforms. This approach reduces adoption friction but also raises questions about lock-in and interoperability. The Cross App Access Protocol and other standards suggest the industry recognizes the need for interoperability, but proprietary agent ecosystems may still emerge.

5. The Agentic Organization Is Emerging

McKinsey published “The agentic organization: contours of the next paradigm” and “One year of agentic AI: six lessons” , arguing that agents aren’t just tools—they’re changing how work gets done. MIT Sloan Management Review published “Agentic AI at scale: redefining management for a superhuman workforce” , examining how organizations must adapt to manage autonomous AI workers.

CIO published articles on “rethinking the IT organization for the agentic AI era” and “taming AI agents: the autonomous workforce of 2026” —reflecting how IT leaders are preparing for agent deployments.

Bessemer Venture Partners published an “AI agent autonomy scale” —a new way to understand use case maturity and agent capabilities.

SaaStr published a practical “AI Agent Playbook” documenting how the company deployed 20+ agents to scale 8-figure revenue with single-digit headcount. Another SaaStr article examined whether AI agents can really manage other agents —concluding that while agent-on-agent management is possible, it creates “more work, not less” in the near term.

From proof of concept to success stories” .

Looking Forward: What Comes Next

September’s developments suggest Q4 2025 will focus on three priorities:

  1. Governance: Enterprises that deployed agents experimentally in Q3 will build governance frameworks in Q4. Control planes, observability platforms, and policy engines will move from nice-to-have to must-have.

  2. Security Hardening: The MCP vulnerabilities will prompt security reviews across agent deployments. Expect enterprises to demand security certifications, penetration testing, and compliance audits before trusting agents with sensitive data.

  3. ROI Proof: With 40% of projects at risk of failure, enterprises will pressure vendors to prove ROI. Results-based pricing models (like Paid’s) will become more common as customers refuse to pay for agents that don’t deliver measurable outcomes.

The honeymoon period for AI agents is ending. September showed that the technology is real—funding is flowing, products are shipping, enterprises are deploying. But the honeymoon is ending, and now comes the hard work of making agents reliable, secure, and valuable at scale.

BCG noted that AI agents are transforming consumer goods, while IBM argued that designing workflows where humans and agents thrive is the key to successful deployment.

Japan’s Tokio Marine and OpenAI announced a partnership on developing AI agents—reflecting international interest in the technology beyond the US market.

The Times predicted “downloadable employees” as the next workforce revolution, while ITPro asked whether workers should prepare to become AI agent bosses.

CNBC reported that companies are spending big on agentic AI “without always knowing what it does”—highlighting the knowledge gap that still exists between agent vendors and enterprise buyers.

AIMultiple published “12 reasons AI agents still aren’t ready in 2026” , while Visionary Marketing offered “AI agents, beyond the hype” —both attempting to ground expectations in reality.

September 2025 was a landmark month for AI agents—not because any single breakthrough occurred, but because the technology moved from concept to deployment at enterprise scale. The funding, product launches, security vulnerabilities, and governance developments all point to an ecosystem that is growing up quickly. The question for Q4 is whether the industry can address the security, governance, and ROI challenges before enterprises lose patience with the experimentation phase.

The infrastructure is being built, the products are shipping, and the money is flowing. Now comes the hard part: making AI agents reliable enough to trust with business-critical work. September showed both the promise and the peril of the agentic future—progress is real, but so are the challenges ahead.
